key_insight: Vision-language models can prioritize textual prompts over visual evidence: when a prompt overstates object counts, models increasingly 'hallucinate' to match the prompt as the true number of objects grows. This reveals a prompt-induced bias that scales with task difficulty.
problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes why and when VLMs favor language priors over image content, causing prompt-induced hallucinations in multimodal outputs (tested in a controlled object-counting setting).
method: Controlled object-counting experiments: present images with known object counts and prompts that deliberately overstate the count to measure model compliance versus visual correctness.
Behavioral and mechanistic analysis: quantify hallucination rates across object counts and probe model internals to isolate reliance on textual priors vs. visual evidence.
Comparative evaluation across models/prompts to show how hallucination scales with count and prompt phrasing.
impact: Clarifies a common failure mode in VLMs and informs safer prompt design, model training, and evaluation strategies to reduce multimodal hallucinations in real-world applications.
visual_elements: Side-by-side example: image + overstating prompt vs. model response (correct vs. hallucinated)
Line chart: hallucination rate (y) vs. ground-truth object count (x) showing increasing conformity to prompt
Schematic: experimental setup flow (image → prompt → model → evaluation) with counted/incorrect outputs highlighted
Heatmap or attention illustration indicating stronger text-conditioned activation than visual features for hallucinated cases
paper_title: Mechanisms of Prompt-Induced Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
paper_authors: William Rudman, Michal Golovanevsky, Dana Arad, Yonatan Belinkov, Ritambhara Singh
